sections.h2: What makes selling a house in Jeffersontown, KY different?
sections.html:
Jeffersontown, known locally as J-town, is a city inside Louisville Metro, so a sale there involves both city and Jefferson County rules. The city bills its own real estate tax and licenses its own businesses, while the Jefferson County Property Valuation Administrator sets the assessment. Sellers who forget the city bill are the ones most often surprised at closing.

The 2020 census counted 28,474 residents on about 10.6 square miles, a density near 2,700 people per square mile, and the July 2025 estimate is 29,193. The city is fully urban and densely built, with 12,083 households and a 5.0% housing vacancy rate in 2020.

sections.h2: What do the Census figures say about Jeffersontown homes?
sections.html:
Typical owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $250,700, according to QuickFacts, and 70.1% of households own. Owners paying a mortgage report $1,601 in median monthly costs, while median rent is $1,320. Household income at the median is $81,506 and per capita income is $41,471.

  • Residents 65 and older: 21.9%, the largest senior share among the four cities in this guide set.
  • Foreign-born residents: 8.7%, and 10.0% of people age 5 and over speak a language other than English at home.
  • Adults with a bachelor's degree or higher: 39.8%.
  • People living in poverty: 6.5%.
  • Retail sales in 2022: about $1.96 billion, or $67,643 per resident, a sign of how many shoppers and workers the city draws from outside.

With a large share of older owners, many Jeffersontown sales come from downsizing and estates, where the house is full of belongings and needs updating before a retail buyer will bid.

sections.h2: Where did Jeffersontown come from, and where is it today?
sections.html:
The settlement began in the late 1700s as a stopover for travelers heading to the Falls of the Ohio at Louisville. A landowner named Bruner petitioned the Jefferson County Fiscal Court in May 1797 to incorporate 40 acres as a town, and residents long called it Brunerstown before Jefferson Town became the name. The Tyler Settlement Rural Historic District, a 600-acre area of preserved farms east of the city, includes the 170-acre Blackacre Nature Preserve used for school programs.

Today the city sits in southeastern Jefferson County and shares five ZIP codes: 40220, 40223, 40269, 40291 and 40299. The skyline is office parks and subdivisions, and Gaslight Square is the historic core.

sections.h2: What is Bluegrass Commerce Park, and why does it matter to sellers?
sections.html:
Bluegrass Commerce Park opened in 1966 on 600 acres and was described as the first such development in the United States. It now covers more than 1,800 acres with roughly 850 businesses and 38,000 jobs, which makes Jeffersontown the third-largest employment center in Kentucky. The park is split into seven units, including Commonwealth Park, Watterson Trail Industrial Park, Plainview Office Park and Blankenbaker Crossings.

That concentration of employment keeps commute times short for nearby owners: the Census mean travel time to work is 21.5 minutes. It also means many houses near the park are bought by people who work within a few miles, which is a point worth making in a listing.

sections.h2: How do city and county property taxes work for a Jeffersontown seller?
sections.html:
The city mails its own real estate tax bill in the first week of October. A 2% discount applies if the bill is paid by October 31, the base amount is due December 31, and on January 1 a one-time 6% penalty is added with 6% annual interest on the unpaid balance. Taxes unpaid on May 1 after the tax year trigger a city lien recorded at the Jefferson County Clerk.

Mortgage companies get copies of every bill, so ask your lender whether the tax comes out of escrow. When property sells, the seller typically pays the buyer a prorated amount for the part of the year the seller owned the house.

sections.h2: What is the deed tax, and who handles exemptions and assessment appeals?
sections.html:
KRS 142.050 puts a deed transfer tax on the grantor at 50 cents per $500 of value, rounded up. The $250,700 median value would produce $251.00. The county clerk collects it at recording, and foreclosure transfers are exempt.

The Jefferson County PVA assesses real property at fair cash value. Owners 65 and older qualify for the homestead exemption, and owners classified as totally disabled qualify for the disability exemption, both applied through the PVA. To contest a value, attend the open inspection period that starts the first Monday in May and runs 13 days, and meet with the PVA before filing an appeal at the clerk's office. The city's own FAQ points to the Jefferson County Clerk's office at (502) 574-5700 as one source for plot information about a lot.

sections.h2: Which Jeffersontown permits and licenses affect a sale?
sections.html:
The city's Department of Permitting and Code Enforcement issues building, trade and demolition permits, and its page says a permit is required to construct, enlarge, alter (including interior demolition), move or change the use of a building, and to install an in-ground pool. A buyer's lender or inspector may ask for proof that past work was permitted.

  • Fences up to 4 feet in front or street-side yards, 8 feet for solid fences and 6 feet for chain link in rear or side yards, need no city permit; corner lots must keep sight lines clear.
  • Home occupations are limited to 10% of the home, two deliveries a day and one non-resident employee.
  • In-ground pools need Metro Health Department approval first, then a city permit, and a four-foot fence with a self-latching gate.
  • Any business operating in the city, which can include contractors on a repair job, must register and pay a $75 annual license fee within 10 days of starting.

If your house has a recent addition, gather the permit and the inspection sign-off before you list it.

sections.h2: How do I sell a Jeffersontown house quickly?
sections.html: Start with a clean paper trail: deed, payoff, city and county tax bills and permit records. Then compare routes. A listing suits an updated house with time to wait for loan approval. A cash sale suits a house with belongings still inside, deferred repairs or an unfinished estate. An investor purchase can keep a tenant in place. Ask for written figures on closing costs and prorations from each buyer before you choose.

faqs.q: Does Jeffersontown have its own property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The city bills a real estate tax separately from Louisville Metro and the county, with bills mailed in early October and a 2% discount through October 31. Ask the Revenue Department at city hall, 10416 Watterson Trail, for a payoff before closing.

faqs.q: What penalties apply to late Jeffersontown real estate tax?
faqs.a: A bill unpaid on January 1 draws a one-time 6% penalty and 6% annual interest, and a lien is filed if it stays unpaid on May 1 of the following year. A lien is released when tax, penalty and interest are paid in full.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed tax on a Jeffersontown sale?
faqs.a: The seller. Under KRS 142.050 the tax is 50 cents per $500 of value, so a sale at $250,700 owes $251.00, and the clerk collects it at recording.

faqs.q: Can a Jeffersontown homeowner age 65 or older get a tax exemption?
faqs.a: Yes. The city's FAQ says the homestead exemption is available to owners 65 and older, and a disability exemption applies to owners classified as totally disabled. Apply through the Jefferson County PVA.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to fence or add a pool before selling in Jeffersontown?
faqs.a: A fence does not need a city permit if it meets the height rules, but an in-ground pool needs Metro Health Department approval and a city permit. Do not start either project unless the work can be finished and inspected before the closing.
